figs.cap: Panels a) and b) show typical S1 and S2 states, composed by t₁- and t₂-vertex, respectively. Namely, note that t₁-vertex appear alternating residual charges, so that the whole system remains magnetically neutral; c) BRASI system composed by two identical layers disposed parallel each other with a height offset, h, between them. The layers may be twisted each other by an angle φ; d) The five vertex types for all possible 16 arrangements of 4 dipoles per vertex; e) Residual charge, Q, or net diagonal magnetic moment, m, locally appear at a vertex as the layer is stretched along one direction (for further details, see Appendix A and Refs. Rectangular-2012 ; RectangularASI-2 ).

How energy density (energy per vertex) behaves with the height offset, h. The layers interact with each other according to a Buckingham-like potential, Eq.(2). Attraction (or repulsion) between them depends on the respective configuration of the bilayer system. Above, we have depicted only the attractive cases, ν(h)<0, by choosing A<0 in Table 1, which means that the layers have opposite dipole configurations.

a) Energy behavior due to the twisting angle between the layers, φ, for a number of γ values (each layer is composed of 841 vertices, leading to a relatively high interaction energy). b) Normalized potential behavior around their respective minima for each γ. The deepest minima occur at γ=√3 composed by t1-vertex yielding stripe-like superlattice pattern (red color), while t2 vertices lead to elongated vortex-type moire pattern (magenta color). The square geometry, γ=1, presents a relatively deep minima with circular moire vortex pattern (black color). In general, as the vortex patterns become elongated, resembling an elliptical shape, their respective minimum become less deep.

Contour plot of the in-plane specific heat c/k_B as a function of interlayer distance h and temperature. In the dark-blue region, the specific heat is essentially zero and no dynamical activity takes place. The red region indicates where the specific heat is most pronounced, corresponding to the occurrence of the order–disorder phase transition.
